facts.raw_span: A man in his 50s with a 10-year history of Crohn disease
intermittent bowel obstructions leading to total proctocolectomy and ileostomy
Five weeks after his surgery, he developed a painful, erosive lesion around his stoma on the anterior abdominal wall
No additional cutaneous or mucosal lesions were present
Repeated cultures were negative
Revealed epidermal erosion with suprabasal epidermal splitting with acantholysis
Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin showed intercellular deposition of IgG and C3 throughout epidermis
Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay showed high level of IgG autoantibodies
Against desmoglein 1: 40 IU/mL (normal value: 20 U/mL)
Against desmoglein 3: 90 IU/mL (normal value: 20 U/mL)
A painful, erosive lesion around the stoma on the anterior abdominal wall
Hematoxylin-eosin stain showing suprabasal epidermal splitting with acantholysis (original magnification ×100)

concepts.why: High levels of IgG autoantibodies against desmoglein 1 and 3, along with intercellular deposition of IgG and C3 throughout epidermis, are characteristic of Pemphigus vulgaris.
The development of a painful, erosive lesion around the stoma site is a known complication of stoma formation.
The presence of autoantibodies and intercellular deposition of IgG and C3 is consistent with an autoimmune bullous disease.
The painful, erosive lesion around the stoma site could be consistent with Pyoderma gangrenosum, a condition often associated with inflammatory bowel disease.
The patient's history of Crohn disease and the development of a skin lesion around the stoma site could be related to the underlying inflammatory bowel disease.
The painful, erosive lesion around the stoma site is consistent with peristomal pyoderma gangrenosum, a condition that can occur in patients with inflammatory bowel disease.
The presence of autoantibodies and intercellular deposition of IgG and C3 is consistent with bullous pemphigoid, although the clinical presentation is more consistent with Pemphigus vulgaris.

The presence of autoantibodies and intercellular deposition of IgG and C3 is consistent with epidermolysis bullosa acquisita, although the clinical presentation is more consistent with Pemphigus vulgaris.

The histopathology finding of suprabasal epidermal splitting with acantholysis, along with the presence of intercellular deposition of IgG and C3 throughout epidermis, is consistent with Pemphigus foliaceus.
